title: Stage-Aware Environmental Setpoints and Risk Review
objective: Build environmental control envelopes from plant stage, measured tissue conditions, facility capability, and documented risk instead of copying a universal chart.

terms.definition: Requested controller value for a measured variable.
Accepted range around a target before corrective action or alarm.
Range in which a controller intentionally avoids switching equipment to limit cycling.
Structured evaluation of plant, quality, safety, equipment, and data consequences before a control change.

coreScience: Environmental targets are coupled. Changing air temperature alters saturation vapor pressure, VPD, leaf energy balance, HVAC load, and possibly dew-point margin. Changing RH changes evaporative demand and condensation risk. Airflow changes boundary layers and distribution. CO2 response depends on light and plant capacity. Setpoints must therefore be designed as a coordinated control envelope.

Stage changes the crop but does not create exact universal numbers. Propagules have limited roots and benefit from restrained demand; established vegetative canopies have greater hydraulic capacity; transition changes canopy density and heat load; flowering increases concealed humidity and disease consequences. Genotype, container, substrate, plant size, PPFD, irrigation, and facility design remain essential.

A robust program separates normal bands, warning limits, action limits, and emergency limits. It also defines measurement locations, persistence time, sensor disagreement rules, equipment staging, alarm routing, manual override, recovery, and crop disposition. Tight targets unsupported by equipment capacity produce cycling and unstable plant conditions.

Coupled physical variables. Air temperature changes saturation vapor pressure; relative humidity and leaf temperature jointly influence estimated leaf-to-air vapor pressure difference. Lighting, air movement and transpiration alter leaf energy balance. One controller adjustment can shift several plant-relevant conditions.
Control dynamics. Deadbands, sensor lag, equipment minimum-run times and capacity limits influence stability. An excessively narrow band may cause cycling without improving crop conditions.

Microclimate and growth stage. Canopy density, root development, transpiration and enclosed flower structures change spatial gradients and risk through development. Stage labels alone do not establish a universal numerical target.

Feedback and risk. Compare logged conditions against the envelope and observed crop response. Escalate sustained excursions through warning, corrective-action and safety pathways. Worker safety limits are independent of crop optimization targets.
cultivationRelevance: Begin with evidence-aware starting envelopes, then qualify them through a room test and crop response. Review leaf temperature, air and leaf VPD, dew-point margin, substrate water use, root health, growth, disease, CO2, and energy demand together.

Approve changes through a written risk review. Alter one primary factor at a time when feasible, preserve the previous qualified recipe, define success and stop criteria, and require a post-change map across lights-on, lights-off, irrigation, and peak-load states.
For each variable, record the control sensor, verification sensors, normal operating band, persistence time, warning/action threshold and safe equipment response.
Map leaf and air temperatures, RH, dew-point margin, light and root-zone measurements during lights-on, lights-off and peak-load conditions.
Change one primary variable at a time when feasible; retain a versioned previous recipe, document effects and roll back if defined stop criteria occur.
Treat any illustrative band or diagram as a workflow example, not a published cannabis-specific temperature, humidity or CO2 prescription.

measureAndRecord.requirement: Stage, variable, normal band, warning, action, emergency limit, location, and persistence.
PPFD, photoperiod, leaf temperature, dew point, VPD method, CO2, irrigation, and airflow.
Capacity, staging, deadband, minimum run time, redundancy, alarm, and fail-safe state.
Plant, quality, disease, worker, energy, condensate, and equipment risks plus mitigations.
Empty-room and occupied maps, crop response, deviations, approval, version, and review date.

For each variable, record the control sensor, verification sensors, normal operating band, persistence time, warning/action threshold and safe equipment response. Map leaf and air temperatures, RH, dew-point margin, light and root-zone measurements during lights-on, lights-off and peak-load conditions.

misconceptions: A stage chart is a universal recipe: It is only a starting hypothesis until qualified for the actual genotype and system.
Tighter control is always better: Unrealistic bands can increase cycling, instability, energy use, and alarm fatigue.
Room setpoint equals plant condition: Leaf, flower, root-zone, and canopy microclimates may differ from the control sensor.
evidenceLimits: This volume intentionally does not publish one cannabis temperature-RH-VPD chart as settled science. Final envelopes require facility qualification, cultivar records, current safety rules, and repeated crop review.
The diagram shows decision flow rather than quantitative control thresholds. Site-specific bands require facility qualification.
A single room sensor may miss leaf, flower and root-zone gradients; sensor calibration and placement errors can exceed apparent improvements.
Published greenhouse response studies do not justify one universal cannabis setpoint chart across cultivars and developmental stages.

overview: An environmental setpoint is a controller request, not a direct measurement of leaf, flower or root-zone conditions. Stage-aware control requires an evidence-informed operating envelope, mapped sensor locations, verified equipment capacity, crop-response observations and a documented process for changes.
